query: ai agent vs automation which one you need
title: AI agent vs automation: which one you need | 50agents
description: Use an automation when the same input should always give the same result, and an AI agent when each case needs judgement. A test and a worked example.
h1: AI agent vs automation: which one you need
answer: Use an automation when the steps are the same every time and the same input should always give the same result, such as copying each new order into a sheet.
Use an AI agent when each case needs judgement about what to do, such as deciding which emails need a reply and writing it; many jobs are an automation with one AI step in the middle.

The AI, on each run, within its instructions
An event (a new order) or a schedule
Usually a schedule or a request

body.p: Anthropic draws the same line: workflows follow paths set in advance, while AI agents direct their own process and tools, which suits problems where you cannot predict the steps. It also warns that an AI agent’s autonomy brings higher cost and the chance of errors compounding.

Take "keep up with new leads". As an automation: every new HubSpot contact becomes a row and a Slack post. It never misses one and never invents one, but it cannot tell a real buyer from a student filling in the form for a class.

As an AI agent: every weekday at 9:00 it reads yesterday’s new contacts, looks at what each wrote, and drafts a first reply to the three that look like buyers. It saves you the reading, and it can be wrong about who is a buyer, so its replies wait for your yes.
Neither is better. The first is a log you can trust; the second is a colleague you check on. Many teams run both.

method.intro: Most real jobs land in between: an automation with one AI step. "When a support email arrives, sort it into billing, bug or question, then add it to the sheet" is fixed steps with one judgement in the middle.

steps.title: Could you write the rule as "when X, do Y"?
steps.body: If yes, build an automation. "When a Stripe payment succeeds, add a row" needs no judgement, and a fixed step will do it the same way every time.

steps.title: Would a different result from the same input be a problem?
steps.body: For payroll, invoices and anything you report on, yes. Keep those as automations, and put judgement only where it helps.

steps.title: Does the input arrive as messy text?
steps.body: Emails, tickets, web pages, notes. Reading those well is what AI is for. OpenAI lists unstructured data, judgement and rules too tangled to maintain as the three signs an AI agent is worth it.

steps.title: Can the judgement live in one step?
steps.body: If only one part needs reading or choosing, make it one AI step inside an automation and keep the rest fixed. It costs less per run and fails in fewer places.

body: In 50agents you do not have to choose up front. Captain, the AI that builds things, picks the kind from what you say and tells you in one line: an automation for fixed steps on an event or a schedule, with AI as a step inside when a step needs judgement; an AI agent when judgement decides what to do on each run. Your own word wins: if you say "automation", it builds one or tells you why it cannot.
example.ask: When a support email arrives, sort it into billing, bug or question and add it to my Support sheet

build.name: Sort support email
build.line: Each support email filed by what it is about
build.when: On each new email to support@
does: An AI step sorts it: billing, bug or question
Adds it as a row to your Support sheet
build.asksFirst: Nothing: it writes to your own sheet

wrong.title: An AI agent where a rule would do
wrong.body: You pay for judgement on every run and get results that vary. If you can write the rule, write the rule.

wrong.title: An automation where judgement was needed
wrong.body: The fixed steps treat every email or lead the same. You end up adding filters for every exception until nobody can follow it. That is the sign to move the judgement to an AI step or an AI agent.

wrong.title: Nobody can say why it did that
wrong.body: With an AI agent, keep its run reports and read them. With an automation, keep its run history. Pick tools that show both.

wrong.title: "Agentic" products that are automations
wrong.body: Some tools sold as AI agents run fixed steps. That is fine if it fits your job; just judge them by what each run does, not by the label.

faqs.q: Is an AI agent just a smarter automation?
faqs.a: No. An automation does what you set up, the same way each time. An AI agent decides what to do within its instructions, so it can handle new cases and also make new mistakes.
Yes. An AI step can write an email, sort a message or pull fields out of text, while the rest of the steps stay fixed.
An automation, almost always, because it does not read and reason on every run. An AI step or an AI agent costs more per run, which is worth it only where judgement saves you time.
